items.title: ASML is quietly building a die-to-wafer hybrid bonder — on a conveyor track
items.idea: 27 bonding patent families filed Dec 2022–Nov 2024, mostly D2W, plus a March report of an architecture design with Prodrive and VDL ETG. Instead of a bond head picking dies, each die rides its own shuttle (SuperTrak-style) past inspection, clean, plasma, metrology and alignment stations, and the chuck lifts the wafer up to the die. Independent shuttles raise station utilization (3 clean stations for a 3s step, 1 bond station for a 1.2s step) and let mixed chiplets share a line via recipe change. SA thinks logic adopts first; premium pricing expected.
items.angle: ASML moving from litho into the back end is vertical integration into the thing that now limits advanced packaging. Direct read-through to Besi and to whoever supplies track/motion.
items.tweetA: Everyone prices ASML as an EUV monopoly. 27 hybrid-bonding patent families says the next monopoly they're after is the step AFTER litho. Packaging is where the bottleneck lives now, and they know it. $ASML $BESI
items.tweetB: Hybrid bonding yield is set by two things: alignment and particles. ASML has spent 20 years selling machines that solve exactly those two problems. The question isn't whether they can build a bonder. It's why Besi's multiple assumed they wouldn't.

charts.desc: Patent drawing of ASML's track-based D2W bonder with stations 210-226 labeled; also ORION alignment-mark asymmetry and post-bond overlay chart (40-60nm down to <4nm). Charts inside — worth opening.

items.title: Bad news for Besi: logic is most of its hybrid-bonding revenue and HBM is slipping to 2029+
items.idea: SA says Besi is the only D2W supplier in volume, but its HB business is concentrated in logic at TSMC and Intel, exactly where ASML has 20 years of relationships and just announced a joint photomask initiative in September. On top of that, SA expects HBM to not adopt D2W hybrid bonding before 2029, if at all, versus a market that expected HBM to be the D2W volume driver from 2028; Korean challengers are also catching up.
items.angle: Two separate hits to one name: share risk in logic and timing risk in HBM. Consensus HBM-HB timeline of 2028 is what SA is explicitly fading.
items.tweetA: Besi's bull case had two legs: logic share and HBM volume from 2028. SemiAnalysis just kicked both at once: ASML walks into TSMC/Intel logic, HBM bonding slides to 2029+. When the sole incumbent in a new tool category gets this note, the multiple is the trade. $BESI $ASML
items.tweetB: Sole supplier in volume is the best position in semicap right up until the day a customer's litho vendor decides to build it. Ask how many times 'only vendor' stayed true after ASML showed up.

items.title: Hybrid bonding numbers: 1um particle kills a 10mm area; D2W today is ~1 wafer/hour; post-bond overlay 40-60nm → <4nm
items.idea: A single 1um particle between full-thickness wafers can unbond ~10mm. Current D2W throughput upper bound is about one wafer per hour, keeping cost per die high. SuperTrak shuttle repeatability is ~10um versus the 50nm placement the bond needs, so final placement is done by holder and chuck. ASML's metrology plus scanner correction already takes post-bond overlay from 40-60nm to below 4nm; NXT:2100i holds 0.9nm overlay.
items.angle: The economics of 3D integration are a cleanliness and throughput story, not a lithography-node story. Cost per die is the real gate for HBM and logic stacking.
items.tweetA: One particle. 10mm of dead bond. That's why hybrid bonding behaves like a front-end process even though it's sold as packaging. Back-end budgets and front-end yield discipline are colliding, and the vendor list is going to look different in 2029.
items.tweetB: One wafer per hour. That's SA's upper bound on D2W bonder throughput in volume today. If that's the bottleneck for 3D stacking, bonder capex has to scale a lot before 'AI packaging' stops being supply-constrained.

charts.desc: Fig 5 particle-induced void; Fig 7 post-bond overlay before/after scanner correction.

items.title: US implied oil demand shows no 'demand destruction' ~8 months into the Iran war
items.idea: Product supplied (a proxy for US plus export-driven global demand) is holding; refineries run near max and exports require foreign demand. The author contrasts this with the 2008 implied-demand chart and says that on historical analogs we're nowhere near destruction levels for developed economies. IEA's claim of -2.5 mb/d lost (0.73 mb/d China) is called a stretch, since ~0.75 mb/d of 2025 China demand was SPR buying, not consumption.
items.angle: Directly bullish-oil and refiner-margin framing against the IEA narrative. If demand is not breaking, the price ceiling is a supply question only.
items.tweetA: IEA says the world has lost 2.5 mb/d of demand. US product supplied, which includes everything we export, says otherwise. Exports can't exist without a buyer. If the demand-destruction thesis is wrong, who's short the crack spread? $VLO $MPC $PSX
items.tweetB: China's SPR buying was ~0.75 mb/d of last year's demand. Strip it out and 'China demand loss' is mostly a base effect from stockpiling that ended. Half of the IEA's demand-destruction number may be a statistical artifact, and the curve is priced as if it's real.

charts.desc: US implied oil demand (product supplied) vs 2008 analog; IEA demand-loss charts. Charts inside — worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Simon White (Bloomberg)
items.title: Watch Taiwan and Korea chip exports, not Treasuries, to time the top in stocks
items.idea: White argues the forces driving yields matter more than the level. Semiconductor exports from Taiwan and South Korea are the early-warning indicator for an AI investment slowdown, potentially turning three to six months before the broader earnings cycle. Even the hot CPI print looks unlikely on its own to break the AI trade.
items.angle: A clean, trackable lead indicator for the AI capex cycle, with a stated 3-6 month lag before earnings.
items.tweetA: Everyone's staring at the 10-year. The cleaner top signal for the AI trade is Taiwan and Korea chip export prints, which lead earnings by 3-6 months. They haven't rolled over yet. When they do, it won't matter what yields are doing.
items.tweetB: Korea got crushed yesterday and TSMC just guided Q4 to $52-54B. Those two facts can't both be the whole story. The export data will settle which one is early.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Simon White (Bloomberg)
items.title: Implied ERP at 3.67% and ~9% expected S&P return with 10-year above 5%
items.idea: Higher real yields have squeezed valuations, but extraordinary earnings expectations still support the rally. Implied equity risk premium is 3.67%, expected S&P 500 returns near 9%, and Treasury yields are above 5%.
items.angle: With 10y above 5%, equities are priced for a ~9% return, roughly 400bp over the risk-free; the whole spread depends on earnings holding.
items.tweetA: Treasuries above 5%. S&P implied return around 9%. You're getting four points for taking full equity risk with earnings revisions as the only support. That works until the earnings estimate for one sector, AI, gets cut.
items.tweetB: The ERP isn't the problem. The denominator is. A 3.67% premium is fine if forward earnings are right, and nearly all the incremental earnings are in the same ten names that credit markets are suddenly doubting.

items.source: Natalie Brunell / The News Block (Eric Balchunas interview)
items.title: Even after a ~50% drawdown from peak, almost all money in Bitcoin ETFs stayed put
items.idea: Balchunas says what matters is how much capital you retain when it gets ugly: Bitcoin funds kept nearly all inflows through a ~50% peak-to-trough drop. He attributes the recent turn to a reminder that Washington steps in to support markets, the original Bitcoin thesis. He recommends a ~3% allocation as 'hot sauce'. BlackRock's fund briefly became its highest revenue-generating ETF of 1,000+.
items.angle: Holder-base quality evidence: ETF flows have become sticky rather than hot money. Also the 'government backstop' narrative as the demand driver.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin ETFs went through a 50% drawdown and almost nobody left. That's not what speculative flows look like. It's what a new strategic allocation looks like. Compare it to what the AI complex's holders just did in a three-day wobble. $IBIT $BTC
items.tweetB: The bull case for Bitcoin this quarter isn't adoption, it's the Fed put, Treasury put and every other put reminding people why a non-sovereign asset exists. Which means the better the policy backstop gets, the stronger the thesis, and the weaker the dollar.

items.title: ~$100M drained from Ledger wallets — tampered devices, not a company hack
items.idea: Per the newsletter, around $100 million has been drained from Ledger hardware wallets; the cause was devices tampered with before reaching owners (supply-chain interdiction), not a breach of Ledger itself. Also covered: warning that AI could soon break Bitcoin's cryptography, which most experts think is overblown.
items.angle: Supply-chain attack on self-custody, a category risk that hits the 'not your keys' thesis hardest. Body gives few details; full video needed.
items.tweetA: $100M gone from Ledger wallets, and the company wasn't hacked. The devices were tampered with before delivery. Self-custody's weakest link was never the cryptography. It was the courier.
items.tweetB: Everyone argues exchanges vs self-custody. Today's data point: you can lose to a supply chain you never saw. Qualified custody with insurance just got a better sales pitch than any ETF ad.

items.title: Quiet Treasury hire: an advocate for tying the dollar to gold
items.idea: The newsletter flags a low-profile Treasury appointment of someone who has argued for years that the dollar should be linked to gold again. Also: Luke Gromen's debate about whether Wall Street 'paper Bitcoin' could cap the price below $1M, with Saylor and Lyn Alden weighing in.
items.angle: Personnel is policy; a gold-standard advocate inside Treasury is a low-probability, high-impact signal for gold and bitcoin, and the paper-BTC argument is a supply-of-claims point.
items.tweetA: A gold-standard advocate got a quiet job at Treasury. Not a signal that anything changes next month. It's the kind of appointment you look back on in five years and say 'the Overton window was moving.' $GLD $BTC
items.tweetB: Gromen's paper-Bitcoin question is the commodity-futures problem all over again: if claims on the asset can be issued faster than the asset, price discovery happens in the claims. Gold lived through that for fifty years.

items.source: Natalie Brunell / The News Block / Cem Karsan via Balchunas
items.title: Government buys stocks after the next crisis — and why retirement dependence makes it likely
items.idea: Balchunas says he independently reached Cem Karsan's forecast that government will eventually buy equities after the next major financial crisis, citing how much of American retirement now depends on the stock market rising. He also labels the current regime 'VOO and Chill', with gold cooling after last year's run.
items.angle: If the equity market is the retirement system, the policy reaction function includes buying equities. That shapes tail-risk pricing and the logic of vol selling.
items.tweetA: If 401(k)s are the pension system, the next crisis response isn't rate cuts. It's the state owning equities. Two independent people landing on this should bother you. It's the BoJ playbook with a bigger float. $SPY
items.tweetB: Backstop expectation is the reason retail won't sell the dip. The risk is that the backstop is priced before it's built. Buying 'VOO and chill' is a bet on a policy put nobody has legislated.

items.title: OpenAI ads: advertisers 20K→60K in ~6 weeks, CPC ~$5 vs $30-50 on Google
items.idea: Per The Information via Parekh: ~140 people work on ads (nearly half hired since July, Meta the main source); advertisers went from ~20,000 late Aug to ~60,000 early Oct; click price ~$5 versus $30-50 on Google for the same business-software clients; ads hit ~$1B run rate in August versus nearly $50B total run rate. The ad team reorganized seven times and may miss the $2.4B 2026 target. ChatGPT has ~1.2B weekly users, <5% on subscription.
items.angle: CPC arbitrage of 6-10x with 1.2B users is the setup for a Google search-ad share fight. The reorgs show execution risk.
items.tweetA: $5 a click on ChatGPT vs $30-50 on Google, for the same software buyers. That's not a price, it's a subsidy to take share. 1.2B weekly users and 95% on free. This is the AdWords moment, with Meta's ad org as the talent pool. $GOOGL $META
items.tweetB: OpenAI is at ~$50B run rate and $1B of it is ads, 2%. If they get to Google-like monetization on even a third of users, the revenue number changes by a factor of ten. The IPO story isn't compute anymore, it's ARPU.

items.title: Anthropic's quarter: $16.8B, up ~50% — growth slowing ahead of pre-Thanksgiving IPO
items.idea: Per The Information: Anthropic showed investors a $16.8B quarter, up nearly 50%, with headline 'Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation'. Parekh notes the mega IPO is 'pre-Thanksgiving' and OpenAI is competing ahead of both IPOs; Codex and ChatGPT are blending against Anthropic's coding/enterprise lead.
items.angle: Growth deceleration at the largest private AI revenue base into an IPO window, with AI credit already wobbling. Valuation multiple vs growth is the debate.
items.tweetA: $16.8B in a quarter and the headline is 'slowing'. A $16.8B quarter is being graded on the second derivative now. IPO windows don't wait for narratives to catch up.
items.tweetB: AI credit is widening, CoreWeave bonds are under 80 cents, and the two largest AI labs are lining up IPOs in the same six weeks. Someone is going to be the marginal buyer of that paper. It won't be the same people who funded the compute.

items.title: Meta's Muse Spark Open: 816B params / 42B active, runs on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios
items.idea: Meta released an open-weight model Parekh describes as the most capable US open-weight to date, 816B total / 42B active parameters, built for coding and agents. It runs locally on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios at ~$10,800 each and up, via an Apple partnership; Daniel Gross is the diplomat. Local means Meta never sees prompts. AMD announced a ~$1,500 local compute product.
items.angle: Frontier-class open weights on ~$22K of desk hardware changes the cost comparison versus cloud inference. Apple becomes AI hardware distribution.
items.tweetA: A near-frontier 816B model on two Mac Studios. About $22K once, versus thousands a month in cloud bills. If your inference cost is the business model, the break-even just moved to 'buy a desk'. $AAPL $META $NVDA
items.tweetB: Meta has the model, Apple has the silicon, nobody has the cloud margin. This partnership is the first evidence that the winners of local AI may be the ones who never sold you tokens.

items.title: TSMC: sixth straight record quarter, ~$46.5B revenue (+41%), Q4 guide $52-54B, and it will run any Terafab plant
items.idea: Net profit up nearly 70% YoY; Q4 guided $52-54B; 2026-28 capex 'significantly higher' than prior three years; adding another 3nm fab in Taiwan; sending teams to check that customers can actually power and finance data centers. Wei told Bloomberg TSMC would work with Musk's Terafab but must control the plants.
items.angle: Supplier checking customers' ability to power and finance is a credit-quality signal from the top of the chain.
items.tweetA: TSMC is sending teams to check whether its customers can power and finance their data centers. The company that sees every AI order is doing credit diligence on its own demand. That tells you what it thinks about the financing stack. $TSM
items.tweetB: Musk wants to build and run the fab. TSMC says it runs any plant or it's not a partnership. Even the richest man alive doesn't get a vote on the only advanced foundry. Pricing power looks like this.

items.title: Apple under Ternus: AI is 'job one', memory shortage called a 'crisis', foldable iPhone Duo from $1,999
items.idea: Ternus took over from Cook on Sept 1; Cook is executive chairman. The new Siri uses an Apple model built on Gemini, on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Ternus calls the memory chip shortage a crisis with all options on the table. iPhone Duo goes on sale tomorrow, deliveries on the 23rd. Apple's bet: personal, private AI across ~2.5B active devices.
items.angle: Memory shortage reaches the largest consumer-hardware buyer; Gemini inside Siri is a Google distribution win.
items.tweetA: Apple's CEO calling the memory shortage a 'crisis' is the quietest bullish memory data point of the month. If the largest buyer can't get the volume it wants at any price, who's setting the contract price? $MU $AAPL
items.tweetB: Apple's AI strategy is built on Gemini and a privacy argument. Meta just made a near-frontier open model run on Apple silicon. Between those two, the winning AI product might run on Apple hardware and be built by neither.

items.title: Iambic's S-1: compute is only ~8 cents of each R&D dollar
items.idea: Iambic priced its IPO at $16 (IAM), raised $150M, closed day one at $18.91 (+18.2%). Of $77.5M 2025 R&D, ~8% went to cloud compute, ~31% to discovery and lab, ~28.5% to clinic and manufacturing, ~third to people. Compute grew from $2.2M (2024) to $6.0M (2025). NVIDIA holds about 3.9%; Lambda trained its Enchant model.
items.angle: A cost-structure sanity check on 'AI drug discovery is a compute story'. The money still goes to wet lab and trials.
items.tweetA: Iambic: NVIDIA owns 3.9%, Lambda trained the model, and 8 cents of every R&D dollar goes to compute. The AI-biotech trade keeps being sold as a GPU story. The S-1 says it's a lab and clinic story. $IAM $NVDA
items.tweetB: If compute is 8% and lab plus clinic is 60%, then 'AI drug discovery' is a capital-intensive lab business with a software multiple. Iambic priced at $896M cap; Recursion and peers carry $1.2-1.7B EV. That's the discount for admitting it.

charts.desc: No chart in email body; tracker linked in article. Charts inside — worth opening.

items.title: The market bought data, not manufacturing: AI-Science Basket +20.5% vs XBI −4.8%
items.idea: From Aug 7 to Oct 15 the basket rose 20.5%, S&P −0.2%, XBI −4.8%, XLV +6.9%; 19 of 20 up, only NVIDIA down (−3.0%). Data makers (ILMN, TXG, TWST, TEM, NTRA) +33.5%; design software (SDGR, Certara) +31.9%; classic instruments +15.3%; bioprocess +9.0%. Excluding Aug 19 (Moderna/Merck Phase 3), the basket is still +12.7% vs XBI −10.1%. The Fed's Sept 16 hike was the first since July 2023.
items.angle: The market sorted tools by what the work produces (discovery data vs manufacturing volume), not by how customers pay.
items.tweetA: AI-science basket +20.5% in ten weeks while XBI fell 4.8%. The winners sell data, not drugs and not GPUs. In AI-bio, the scarce input turned out to be measured biology. Sequencers beat NVIDIA. $ILMN $TEM $TWST
items.tweetB: Strip one day, Moderna/Merck's mRNA cancer trial hit, and the data-maker lead over instruments shrinks from 18 points to 6. A thesis that depends on one binary readout is half beta and half a trade.

items.title: Iambic: more experiments, each cheaper — and a candidate designed without a co-crystal structure
items.idea: The S-1 describes plate-based chemistry workflows making hundreds of compounds per program weekly, 8 programs now and up to 25 in 2027, and a lease expansion from ~12.5K to ~96K sq ft. It names Anthropic and OpenAI as competitive pressure. It designed one candidate without a high-resolution co-crystal structure, which cuts against the author's NMR/cryo-EM/Bruker moat claim (an inference, filing never mentions them).
items.angle: AI structure prediction substituting for structural instruments is a possible disruption to Bruker-like moats, still thin evidence.
items.tweetA: Iambic designed a drug candidate without a co-crystal structure. If models can supply the structure, the expensive instruments that make structures lose a customer. $BRKR
items.tweetB: Notice who the S-1 treats as competitors: Anthropic and OpenAI. A drug company listing frontier labs as competitive risk is a fresh way to say the labs are moving into science.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Jensen defended CoreWeave and the AI complex bounced, but CoreWeave bonds traded below 80 cents
items.idea: Asia sold off (Korea crushed), US futures were ugly and AI credit was widening. Jensen Huang's defence of CoreWeave's financial position lifted the NeoCloud group. CoreWeave bonds have traded below 80c, CDS widened materially. The author's frame: the market is separating AI demand from the quality of financing structures. A trader quote: 'look at AI credit!!'
items.angle: AI-capex financing is now the stress point. Credit is discriminating by issuer, which changes funding costs for every next cluster.
items.tweetA: Jensen defended CoreWeave and the NeoClouds bounced. The bonds are below 80. When the equity is rescued by the vendor, and the credit isn't, believe the credit. $CRWV $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia is both the supplier and the credibility backstop for its own customer. If your demand needs your CEO to vouch for your customer's balance sheet, you've already told me the answer.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Treasuries rallied on hot PPI, firm data and higher oil: 'bonds be bonds' again
items.idea: Producer inflation hot, growth firm, oil higher, yet long-dated Treasuries rallied hard as safe-haven demand overwhelmed inflation. The author calls it the first convincing evidence in a while of the old equity-bond hedge. The dollar weakened and gold and bitcoin rose, which is read as positioning and cross-asset hedging, with 'bonds, stocks and crude completely decoupled'.
items.angle: A hedge-regime signal: duration works as protection again when the fear is credit, not inflation.
items.tweetA: Hot PPI, higher oil, and the long end rallied anyway. For two years bonds sold off with equities. One day of the opposite is a data point, but a credit scare is the thing that flips the correlation. Check the 60/40 sign. $TLT
items.tweetB: Dollar down, yields down, gold and bitcoin up on a hot PPI day. That's not an inflation trade or a growth trade. It's markets pricing tighter financial conditions without the Fed.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Deutsche Bank
items.title: Rotation out of tech averages 67 days (median 59), drawdown 16.6% (median 14.6%)
items.idea: The Dow, small caps and equal-weight S&P (+~1.4%) outperformed while semis were on a seven-day losing streak. Citing DB, since mid-2024 the average tech rotation ran ~67 days with a mean mega-cap growth drawdown of 16.6% (median 14.6%). The author reads it as a rotation inside leadership rather than index break.
items.angle: Gives a base rate to size the AI-complex drawdown. If it's average, we're early.
items.tweetA: Average tech rotation since 2024: 67 days, 16.6% drawdown. We're a few days in. Equal-weight +1.4% in a day says money is moving, not leaving. Pairs, not shorts. $QQQ $RSP
items.tweetB: The question isn't whether this rotation ends. It's whether the average holds when the credit leg is part of it. Past rotations didn't have CoreWeave at 80.

charts.desc: DB chart of rotation duration and drawdown (see DC Lite #705).

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Warsh heads into Bangkok with credit doing part of the Fed's tightening
items.idea: The author argues an October hike looks less straightforward: inflation says don't get comfortable, but financial conditions are tightening in AI-exposed parts of the system and long yields plus credit are doing some of the work. Crude is rising while PPI is hot, which could revive the inflation channel.
items.angle: The Fed's reaction function now includes AI-credit stress. Hike odds are falling (see DC Lite).
items.tweetA: Warsh doesn't need to hike if CoreWeave's bond curve does it for him. The tightening is coming from credit, not the funds rate. That's a different thing to hedge. $CRWV $SPY
items.tweetB: Oil up, PPI hot, credit widening. The nightmare isn't a hike, it's stagflation-lite where the Fed can't ease because of oil and can't hike because of credit.

items.title: DOJ turns a thumb-drive suspect list into an emergency suit to block ~20,000 California mail ballots
items.idea: After Judge Sooknanan on Oct 9 barred DOJ's collection of unredacted state voter rolls, DOJ sued California to block counting ballots from ~20,000 people it says may be noncitizens, after giving state and county officials 48 hours to investigate a list and set ballots aside. The author's thesis: a narrow case can travel farther, because the burden to disprove shifts to the state; watch the false-positive rate after Nov 3.
items.angle: Election-process risk and a template (federal list, short deadline, emergency relief) that can be reused across states before November 3.
items.tweetA: The court said DOJ can't take the voter rolls. So DOJ brought the list instead, with a 48-hour deadline. Same machinery, reverse order. The thing to watch isn't the ruling, it's the false-positive rate on those 20,000 names.
items.tweetB: Rate limiting by court order worked for the database. It doesn't work for a list with a deadline. If the template works once, every contested state gets a version before the next cycle. Election-risk premium belongs in the vol surface.

items.title: Ripple Prime adds 24/7 swaps on equities, ETFs, metals, energy and FX referencing Hyperliquid perps
items.idea: Per The Block via the newsletter: Ripple Prime launched round-the-clock swaps tied to equities, ETFs, metals, energy and currencies that reference perpetual futures listed on Hyperliquid.
items.angle: Prime-broker access to on-chain perps as a reference price is a piece of TradFi/DeFi plumbing; 24/7 pricing of equities during Asian tape events.
items.tweetA: A prime broker is now offering swaps that reference Hyperliquid perps on equities and oil. The 24/7 price for $SPX risk may be setting on a venue most desks don't have a screen for. $XRP $HYPE
items.tweetB: Asia sold off before the US open this week. If the 24/7 reference price for that move lives on-chain, TradFi will end up using the DeFi tape for overnight price discovery and pretend it didn't.

items.title: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries; Partners Group cuts PE staff with shares −40% YTD
items.idea: Things-happen items: Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries (Foreign Policy). Partners Group cut dozens from its private-equity team amid redemption pressure, with shares down 40% this year. Also: Trump canceled the planned livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution, the first US military execution in 60+ years; a Florida civil suit accuses Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking (denied).
items.angle: Refinery strikes are a product-crack-spread input; PE manager redemption stress is a private-credit canary.
items.tweetA: Ukraine hits refineries again. Product shortages, record cracks, and now more Russian capacity offline. The crack spread isn't a bet on demand, it's a bet on Ukraine's drone budget. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: Partners Group down 40%, cutting staff on redemptions. The listed PE managers are the public mark on private marks. When the wrapper trades at a discount to its NAV, believe the wrapper.

items.title: October hike odds fall from 53% to <30% after CPI as Treasuries rally
items.idea: FedWatch probability of an October hike peaked at 53% after the CPI print, then fell below 30% amid a strong Treasury rally and dovish Fed pushback.
items.angle: A 23-point swing in one day on one Treasury rally; the front end is trading credit stress and Fed pushback.
items.tweetA: 53% to under 30% in 24 hours. The Fed didn't change its mind, the credit market did. If one bond rally moves hike odds 23 points, the real reaction function is a long-bond chart.
items.tweetB: Odds above 50% after CPI and then under 30%. That isn't the Fed, that's a market with no conviction about the data. Be careful trading the first print on either side.

items.source: Daily Chartbook (DC Lite) / Goldman via ZeroHedge
items.title: Hedge funds dumped global AI stocks at the second-largest pace of the past year; long sales 3.5x short sales
items.idea: Goldman data: the latest session saw the second-largest net selling in global AI stocks of the past year, behind only the Situational Awareness blow-up in July. Long sales outpaced short sales 3.5 to 1. ZeroHedge headline: net leverage slides for a sixth day.
items.angle: Positioning shock plus de-grossing; most selling by long sales means real exit, not shorts.
items.tweetA: Hedge funds sold global AI at the second-fastest pace this year, with 3.5 long sales for every short. That's a de-gross, not a hedge. Only the Situational Awareness blow-up was bigger. $NVDA $SMH
items.tweetB: Situational Awareness in July, this in October: two de-risking events in the same trade within three months. The question is whether the next one finds a bid.

charts.desc: Goldman chart of hedge fund net selling in AI stocks.

items.title: Old Era stocks have price-beta of zero to a New Era collapse
items.idea: Paulsen: unlike 2000, any New Era stock collapse may not hurt the broad market as much because the price-beta of Old Era stocks is currently zero. Separately DB shows MCG and Tech positioning has cooled but remains crowded relative to the rest.
items.angle: If true, rotation can absorb a tech drawdown without an index crash. The opposite risk is that zero beta flips under liquidation.
items.tweetA: Paulsen: Old Era stocks currently have zero beta to New Era stocks. In 2000 the old-economy cushion didn't exist the way it does now. Zero beta works until everyone sells everything for cash. $RSP $IWM
items.tweetB: The 1998-2000 analog people keep posting misses one thing: breadth. The index can be flat while the leaders fall 30%. That's an alpha environment, not a beta environment.

items.title: HBM test equipment: prices rising from $6M to $10-12M per tester? Advantest vs Teradyne, CXMT localization
items.idea: Only the question list is visible, but it frames the live debates: whether memory-test equipment prices rose from US$6M to US$10-12M, why test machines aren't getting pricier despite HBM demand, why Advantest beat Teradyne in memory, how many CP/FT testers per 100,000 wafers (~$150M investment excluding burn-in), how deep Changchuan has penetrated CXMT, and whether Korean makers will cultivate local test vendors.
items.angle: Test equipment is the least-covered chokepoint in HBM stacking; per-layer test time scales with stack height.
items.tweetA: Everyone has a view on HBM supply. Almost no one has a view on test time per stack. More layers means longer test, which means more testers, which is an Advantest capacity story. $ATEYY $TER
items.tweetB: Chinese memory (CXMT) buys domestic testers like Changchuan and Korean vendors get fostered by Samsung and SK Hynix. Test equipment may become the first place the US-China memory bifurcation shows up in order books.
